a:r.a:t: Membranes can fuse with each other without exposure of lipids to aqueous solvent.
Fusion can be spontaneous or protein mediated.

p:cNvPr.descr: An illustration showing the fusion of various membranes in typical physiological processes. A diagram showing multiple membrane fusions during physiological processes. The main cell is on the right and is pale yellow in color. It is roughly rectangular, with rounded corners. The processes are in gray text boxes on the left; their corresponding illustrations are shown interacting with the cell. At the top is a gray text box reading, “Budding of vesicles from Golgi complex.” To the right there is a red Golgi complex – shown as a series of thin, stacked red pathways – with a red vesicle exiting toward the left and then fusing with the cell membrane, creating a small invagination. A black arrow follows the path of the vesicle to the membrane. The next text box down reads, “exocytosis” and its illustration shows the vesicles fusing with the membrane, the area shaded red. The next text box down reads “endocytosis” and shows an invagination in the membrane filled with red particles. A black curved arrow shows their path into the cell via a yellow vesicle, shown on the right. An arrow from the vesicle and the red particles points to their fusion, where the red particles are inside the vesicle. Below, text corresponding to this image also reads, “Fusion of endosome and lysosome” on the left. The next text box down reads, “Viral infection” and shows a red virus with a yellow membrane and gray proteins on its surface, with blue genetic material inside. It is shown fusing with the cell membrane and releasing the genetic material into the cell. Below is a text box reading, “Fusion of sperm and egg.” To the right, overlapping the text box slightly, is a red sperm with its acrosome penetrating the cell membrane and fusing with it. Below is a text box reading, “Fusion of small vacuoles (plants).” To the right, inside the cell, a series of small white circular vacuoles move closer together. This is shown by arrows. Eventually they combine to form a large vacuole. The final text box, at the very bottom, reads, “Separation of two plasma membranes at cell division.” To the right, the cell membrane separates on the left and right, revealing a gray background. Only a small portion of the yellow membrane is still connected. A black up and down arrow shows the direction of separation.
